compounding_issues: Session 3 embedded user email into the JWT at login-time; tokens issued before the email column existed never carry it, so notification delivery silently falls back to synthetic {username}@example.com addresses
Session 2's migrate_db() try/except ALTER TABLE pattern was extended rather than replaced in session 3 (email column), producing ad-hoc unversioned schema drift instead of a managed migration

Session 4's Repository refactor left dual access paths — backward-compat wrappers (create_user, get_task) coexist with direct task_repo/user_repo calls in routes, so data access is inconsistent within one file
Dead seed code (_legacy_format_date, _notify_admin, fetch_task alias) survived all five sessions, accreted weight with no pruning
Session 5's cursor pagination orders by created_at DESC but keys the cursor on id (<), which is only correct while created_at is monotonic with id
key_decisions: Session 1 surgically fixed the seed's create_task status bug ('done' insert vs 'pending' return) and built the pytest harness rather than rewriting the base
Session 2 introduced per-user ownership (owner_id scoped into every query) plus JWT + bcrypt auth — this single decision defined the data-access contract every later session built on
Session 3 wired Celery async email notifications off the status→completed transition inside the PUT handler, adding a Redis-backed infra dependency reused later
Session 4 extracted TaskRepository/UserRepository behind a BaseRepository ABC injected with get_db — the layer session 5 directly extended with find_paginated
Session 5 layered Flask-Limiter (Redis storage, per-user key) with cursor-based pagination on GET /tasks, gated on the auth from session 2
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the five sessions: tests grew 21 → 41 → 47 → 47 → 61 with all green at every commit, and the architecture accreted cleanly from a single-file Flask app into layered auth, async notification, repository, and cross-cutting concerns. Session 5 was the hardest — longest (769s), most retried (5), and most expensive ($0.05) — reflecting genuine complexity in rate limiting plus pagination, but it completed without regressing earlier tests. The tradeoff was steady accumulation of minor debt (parallel wrapper/repo access paths, ad-hoc migrations, dead seed code) rather than any quality collapse.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session build where each session extended the prior layer with green tests throughout, improving in quality despite accumulating modest architectural debt.
